claims.text: Combining enhanced free-energy sampling with machine-learned interatomic potentials will enable efficient prediction of melting properties across a broad range of high-entropy alloys.
The proposed approach will predict melting temperature with less than 5% error.
The proposed approach will predict enthalpy and entropy of fusion with less than 5% error.
The proposed approach will predict volume change at melting and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties with less than 5% error.
The target initial state is a solid high-entropy alloy near its melting point.
The sampling framework will rigorously explore configurational and compositional spaces.
The simulations will explicitly treat solid-liquid coexistence using machine-learned interatomic potentials.
The approach is applicable to diverse alloy compositions when the interatomic potentials are well calibrated.
Explicit representation of a solid-liquid interface and phase coexistence ensures proper capture of configurational disorder.
Explicit representation of a solid-liquid interface and phase coexistence ensures proper capture of latent-heat effects.
Enhanced free-energy sampling directly computes a full free-energy landscape that includes metastable and coexistence states.
The computed free-energy landscape permits high-precision derivation of latent heats.
The computed free-energy landscape permits high-precision derivation of volume discontinuities at melting.
The predicted melting and liquid properties will agree with high-precision experimental measurements within 5%.
Direct calorimetric measurements are low-throughput across extensive high-entropy-alloy composition spaces.
CALPHAD has low efficiency for exploration of the full composition and temperature space of multicomponent systems.
Equilibrium CALPHAD modeling is insufficiently accurate across extensive compositional spaces.
Failure of machine-learning calibration to capture crucial atomic interactions can limit the approach.
Potential-calibration errors and incomplete sampling convergence are the primary sources of uncertainty.
Deviation exceeding 5% from experiments across multiple high-entropy-alloy compositions would falsify the approach.
